solution.concept_anchor: Bilateral contentious issues prohibited in SAARC forums
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students may reason that a human rights issue (a global norm) should override a regional organisation's internal rules — conflating SAARC's charter rules with UN General Assembly procedures.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves a member state attempting to raise a bilateral political grievance at a SAARC forum — identify the applicable SAARC Charter rule.
Recall: SAARC Charter explicitly prohibits bilateral and contentious issues from being raised in SAARC forums.
Eliminate option (b): The Charter does not allow majority vote to override this prohibition — consensus would be required and the prohibition itself is structural.
Eliminate option (c): Human rights framing does not override SAARC's bilateral issues prohibition — SAARC has no human rights enforcement mechanism.
Eliminate option (d): No special committee mechanism exists in SAARC to address bilateral disputes.
Confirm option (a): The Charter's explicit prohibition on bilateral and contentious issues means the agenda item cannot be raised — this is a fundamental structural rule.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in option (c) expands the human rights framing to suggest it overrides SAARC's internal charter rules. Students aware of international human rights norms may reason that a 'humanitarian' issue should be discussable anywhere. However, SAARC's Charter prohibition on bilateral contentious issues is absolute within the SAARC framework — no human rights exception exists. This tests precise knowledge of SAARC's charter provisions vs. general international law principles.
solution.final_explanation:
SAARC's Charter contains a structural prohibition that limits the organisation's scope in a fundamental way — bilateral and contentious issues cannot be raised at SAARC forums.

Applicable principle: Article of the SAARC Charter prohibits raising bilateral and contentious issues at SAARC meetings — this acts as a structural filter ensuring SAARC focuses on cooperation rather than conflict.

• Option (a) — The agenda item cannot proceed due to the Charter's prohibition on bilateral and contentious issues: Correct. The SAARC Charter's explicit prohibition means no procedural mechanism can admit this item — it is structurally barred.
• Option (b) — A two-thirds majority can override the prohibition: Incorrect. SAARC uses consensus, not majority voting. Even if majority voting were available, the Charter prohibition would require consensus to amend.
• Option (c) — Human rights framing qualifies it as a non-bilateral issue: Incorrect. SAARC has no human rights enforcement mechanism and the Charter's prohibition covers any contentious bilateral matter regardless of framing.
• Option (d) — A special bilateral committee is established: Incorrect. No such mechanism exists under the SAARC Charter.

Value Addition:
• SAARC's bilateral issues prohibition means the Kashmir dispute, Rohingya crisis, or any bilateral tension cannot be formally tabled.
• This rule has been both praised (keeping SAARC from becoming adversarial) and criticised (preventing SAARC from solving regional problems).
• The rule is why SAARC summits rarely produce substantive political outcomes despite significant diplomatic attendance.

solution.concept_anchor: SAARC summit frequency rule vs. reality; 18th summit and Neighbourhood First

statement_analysis.statement: The SAARC Charter mandates that summits be held annually, but in practice, summits have been held irregularly with multi-year gaps — reflecting the gap between the Charter's aspirational timeline and political reality.
statement_analysis.reason: The SAARC Charter prescribes annual summits, but the 19th Summit (last scheduled) has not been held since 2014's 18th Summit — a 10-year gap that starkly illustrates the charter-practice divergence.

statement_analysis.statement: The 18th SAARC Summit held in Kathmandu in 2014 was Prime Minister Modi's first multilateral foreign engagement as head of government.
statement_analysis.reason: PM Modi invited SAARC leaders to his swearing-in ceremony in May 2014 and then attended the 18th SAARC Summit in Kathmandu in November 2014 — the summit is considered his first formal multilateral engagement.

statement_analysis.statement: The diplomatic boycott of the 19th SAARC Summit in 2016 was led exclusively by India — no other SAARC member formally withdrew its participation.
statement_analysis.reason: Multiple SAARC members withdrew — Bangladesh, Bhutan, and Afghanistan also announced non-participation, not just India. The boycott was multi-member, not India-led exclusively.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because the Uri attack narrative centres on India's withdrawal, making it easy to overlook that Bangladesh, Bhutan, and Afghanistan also withdrew — the multi-member nature of the boycott is underreported.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: SAARC Charter mandates annual summits — the gap since 2014 (18th Summit) confirms the charter-practice divergence. Correct.
Statement 2: Modi's Kathmandu 2014 summit as first multilateral engagement — this is consistent with the Neighbourhood First narrative. Correct.
Statement 3: The 2016 boycott was NOT India-led exclusively — Bangladesh, Bhutan, and Afghanistan also withdrew. The statement's 'exclusively by India' is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3's partial truth is that India did lead the narrative of the 2016 boycott — but the 'exclusively' qualifier makes it false. Bangladesh, Bhutan, and Afghanistan also withdrew, making it a multi-member diplomatic signal. Students who have read about the India-Pakistan dimension of the boycott may miss that three other members also withdrew — the multi-country nature of the boycott is a precise fact that distinguishes genuinely prepared students.
solution.final_explanation:
SAARC's summit history and the events around the 19th Summit cancellation are frequently tested.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The SAARC Charter prescribes annual summits, but the organisation has gone through long periods without one. The 19th Summit was last scheduled for 2016 and remains unheid — demonstrating the profound gap between the Charter's aspirational framework and political reality.
• Statement 2 — Correct: PM Modi invited all SAARC heads at his May 2014 swearing-in — a symbolic Neighbourhood First signal. The 18th SAARC Summit in Kathmandu (November 2014) followed as his first formal multilateral summit appearance.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The 2016 boycott was not India-exclusive. India announced withdrawal first, but Bangladesh, Bhutan, and Afghanistan followed — reflecting a broader multilateral signal against Pakistan-based cross-border terrorism, not merely India's bilateral grievance.

Value Addition:
• The SAARC swearing-in diplomacy (May 2014) was unprecedented — no Indian PM had invited SAARC leaders to his inauguration before Modi.
• The 19th Summit remains the last scheduled SAARC summit — a symbol of the organisation's effective paralysis post-2016.
• Bhutan and Bangladesh's boycott signals that smaller members are capable of independent diplomatic positioning.
